headline: Motion to approve appeal over revoked building permit at 35 Congress Street failed 0-5; zoning requests at four other addresses were approved or continued.
summary: The board heard an appeal of the Building Commissioner's decision to revoke a building permit for a Shetland Park unit. The proposed use was disputed, with the petitioner calling it an allowed business office use and the city saying it does not fit that category. The motion to approve the appeal failed.
decisions: Motion to approve the appeal of the revoked building permit at 35 Congress Street, Shetland Park Building 2, Unit 2120, failed 0 in favor and 5 opposed.
Approved variances for a fence at 56 Highland Avenue, with the fence height at the corner lowered, by a 4-1 vote.
Continued the variance petition for 7 Burnside Street and 5 Skerry Street Court to October 21, 2026, by a 5-0 vote.
Approved a variance to construct a 21-foot-tall garage with an accessory dwelling unit at 22 Vista Avenue, by a 5-0 vote.
Approved an amendment to the December 11, 2023 decision for 75 North Street, removing the special condition that barred assigning parking spaces to individual units or residents, by a 5-0 vote.
Approved a special permit to add a second story to the nonconforming house at 8 Conners Road, by a 5-0 vote.
Approved the minutes of the August 19, 2026 meeting as drafted.

City of Salem Zoning Board of Appeals 
DRAFT Meeting Minutes 
September 16, 2026 
 
A meeting of the Salem Zoning Board of Appeals (“Salem ZBA”) was held on Wednesday, 
September 16, 2026, at 6:30 pm via remote participation in accordance with Section 30A of Chapter 20 of 
the Acts of 2021, as amended by Section 40 of Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2023, and further amended by Section 1 
of Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025. The City is authorized to conduct remote meetings of its public bodies 
through June 30, 2027.  
 
Chair Vyedin calls the meeting to order at 6:30 pm. 
Chair Vyedin explains how individuals can participate in the meeting remotely via Zoom, and that 
instructions to participate remotely can also be found on the Salem website.  Ms. Vyedin also 
explains the rules regarding public comment. 
 
ROLL CALL  
Those present were: Chair Nina Vyedin, Vice Chair Christa McGaha, Ellen Simpson, Peter Habib, 
Elena Eimert, and Stephen Larrick.  Also in attendance were Brennan Postich — Staff Planner, Gail 
Kubik — Building Inspector, Omar Bennani — Assistant City Solicitor, and Voula Orfanos — 
Building Commissioner.  Those absent were: Hilary Forbes. 
 
REGULAR AND CONTINUED PETITIONS   
Location: 35 Congress Street Shetland Park Building 2, Unit 2120 (Map 34, Lot 0448) 
(Industrial Zoning District; Coastal Resiliency Overlay District; Waterfront 
Industrial Overlay District) 
Applicant: Prime Group Shetland Park, LLC, and Alessandro Mazzotta 
Project: A public hearing for all persons interested in the petition of PRIME GROUP 
SHETLAND PARK, LLC and ALESSANDRO MAZZOTTA regarding the property 
located at 35 CONGRESS STREET, SHETLAND PARK BUILDING 2, UNIT 
2120, (Map 34, Lot 0448) (Industrial Zoning District; Coastal Resiliency Overlay 
District; Waterfront Industrial Overlay District) to appeal the Building Commissioner’s 
decision to revoke a building permit for that property, including on the basis that the 
proposed use is a data center, a not permitted use per Section 3.1 Principal Uses of the 
Salem Zoning Ordinance. The petitioners contend that the proposed use is allowed as-
of-right and the appeal requests that the Board: 1) reinstate the building permit to allow 
construction under the original scope of work, and 2) direct the Building Department 
to either review the expanded scope of work for building code compliance, or to 
review a new building permit application with instructions that the expanded scope of 
work cannot be denied based on the proposed use. 
 
 
Documents and Exhibitions

Chair Vyedin introduces the petition and explains that, as this is an appeal, the petitioner will have 
time to present, after which the Board will ask questions, then the City Building Department will 
also have time to present, after which the Board will ask questions, followed by public comment. 
 
Attorney Gary Ronan introduces himself on behalf of the petitioner and explains that the petitioner 
believes their building permit, which has been revoked, should be reinstated.  Mr. Ronan asks that 
the Building Department consider the expanded version of the petitioner’s project, either under this 
or a new application if necessary.  Mr. Ronan presents a site plan of the property highlighting the 
project location.  Mr. Ronan states it is a small tenant space in Shetland Park that was previously 
occupied, and that there will be no construction other than interior renovation of an existing space 
in the building.  He also presents a floor plan of a buildout that was approved with the building 
permit.  Mr. Ronan explains the floor plan and operations and notes a future tenant space that was 
part of the unit and originally not proposed to be built out.  Renderings and diagrams of the 
proposed project are shown, describing it as an IT services office with desks and a conference room.  
Mr. Ronan indicates this is an industrial district, and that the use is allowed in the district.  Mr. 
Ronan contends the space will be used for the delivery of low-latency inference computer services to 
customers, which he explains is something that helps with the delays associated with connections to 
various servers, particularly for emergency services, self-driving cars, and other things where the 
latencies matter.  Mr. Ronan states this business operation would offer low-latency computing to 
businesses in and around Salem.  He argues that this is not an AI data center to assist with things 
like ChatGPT.  Mr. Ronan discusses zoning in the Industrial Zoning District and states there is an 
allowed-by-right use for business or professional offices.  He explains this category in detail and 
asserts that the business is providing a qualified service under the category.  Mr. Ronan further 
suggests the Building Department seemed to have initially agreed because they issued a building 
permit.  He explains that on June 23rd there was a site visit where Building Department 
representatives came to inspect the site.  During this visit, the construction team raised with the 
department that there would be a petition to increase the size of the buildout.  Mr. Ronan states the 
only change was to be an increase into the future tenant space previously noted, and to provide 
additional cooling and electrical support for the space.   Mr. Ronan next presents revised floor plans 
showing the proposed expansion and describes the changes, but states that there is no change in the 
underlying proposed use.  On July 6th, the Building Department presented its revocation letter, 
which stated that the changes were substantive enough to warrant a new building permit application, 
and revoked the initial permit under the suspicion that this was no longer, in fact, an IT services 
company use under the allowed use, but rather a data center, which is disallowed.  Mr. Ronan 
explains the appeal of the Building Department’s decision, and suggests the decision was wrong 
because: 1) the use is allowed by right as a common professional business office use; 2) it was based 
on the incorrect assumption that this is a data center, which he argues it is not; and 3) -. 
 
Robert Moser, founder, principal, and CEO of Prime Group, interrupts Mr. Ronan to further 
explain what a low-latency inference computer service is.  Mr. Moser states it is for rapid response 
for triage, for police responses and emergency communications, as well as other vital applications 
that cannot have delays between request and response.  He states there are many differences 
between an AI data center and an inference point, such as the equipment that is used, and states it is 
mainly the execution of applications that are already being used, but that it would reduce latency to 
five to ten milliseconds.  Mr. Moser suggests the proposal would be a huge economic boom for the 
City because it would draw in more companies that require such low latency services.  He suggests 
the impact could be over $1 billion over a ten-year period, and that 600 jobs could be created by 
companies that would want to move in and take advantage of the low latency.  Mr. Moser
City of Salem Zoning Board of Appeals 
September 16, 2026 DRAFT Meeting Minutes 
  3 
characterizes the services as the “last mile compute,” reducing delay.  Mr. Moser also contends that 
the services do not use water like a data center.  He explains there is a closed-loop water system that 
is not connected to the sewer or utility systems.  Mr. Moser suggests this could provide 
opportunities in healthcare, education, manufacturing, and other areas. 
 
Chair Vyedin asks clarifying questions about what inference means in this situation.  Mr. Moser 
indicates it has to do with responses to questions.  She asks which chip is being used, and Mr. Moser 
states he does not know specifically, but that it is an NVIDIA chip.  Chair Vyedin notes there can be 
a big difference in power use depending on the type of chip.  Jonathan Krausche of Prime Group 
introduces himself and states it would depend on the specific tenants, but that it could be NVIDIA 
Vera Rubin or GB300 chips that sit on a typical rack.  He indicates they will be efficient with their 
use of power and keep it to 2.5 megawatts, where the previous tenant used 3 megawatts on average.  
Chair Vyedin confirms that there are no training-use chips.  Ms. Vyedin also asks additional 
questions about the space and use.  Mr. Moser indicates the closest location offering this service is in 
Austin, Texas, and that this would help reduce latency for local uses.  Mr. Moser states the proposal 
is to provide the space, and a tenant will provide the inference.  Chair Vyedin asks about employees, 
and the petitioners indicate there would be about 20 full-time employees.  Chair Vyedin asks 
clarifying questions about the differences between the original and revised plans, as well as which 
spaces in the floor plan will be for servers and which will be used by humans.  Mr. Ronan compares 
the two plans.  Chair Vyedin asks how much of Shetland Park is owned by Prime Group, and Mr. 
Moser indicates they own all of the buildings, of 1.5 million square feet.  Ms. Vyedin next asks about 
expenses incurred between the permit being granted initially and when it was revoked.  Mr. Moser 
indicates that buildout has begun, and that they are fearful of losing a multimillion-dollar 
client/tenant.  Chair Vyedin asks to see the permit application and also asks if the specific proposed 
services were clearly discussed with the Building Department prior to initial approval.  She also asks 
about the difference in power use between a regular CPU or power server and an inference chip.  
Mr. Moser states it would be governed based on the specific use and power cap.  Mr. Moser further 
discusses differences between the proposed use and an AI data center.  Chair Vyedin expresses 
concerns about the similarities, and Mr. Moser retorts that it is equivalent to saying anything with 
four wheels is a race car.  Chair Vyedin asks if low-latency inference computing services are listed as 
an approved use under the Salem Zoning Ordinance, and Mr. Ronan states it is not, but insists that 
this qualifies as a business or professional office, which is an allowed use.  He also states that “data 
center” is not a defined term in the Zoning Ordinance, and that the proposal should be allowed as a 
use that falls under a category that is allowed.  Chair Vyedin next asks if there are any other 
businesses offering this service in Salem.  Mr. Moser states that some hospitals have their own low-
latency systems but that he is otherwise unaware. 
 
Ms. Simpson suggests the first plans look like an office use with a server room to support the office 
use, and that the revised plans seem to be primarily a large number of servers being supported by a 
small number of people.  Ms. Simpson questions why the petitioner would risk the large sum of the 
permit cost to then substantially change the use.  Mr. Moser contends that the future tenant space 
was always indicated, but it was not known at the time what the use would be.  Mr. Moser asks if 
this comes down to a question of the number of computers a business uses.  Chair Vyedin clarifies 
that this is about square footage, as well as primary versus accessory uses.  Chair Vyedin also asks 
that Mr. Moser refrain from interrupting Board members while they are speaking.  Ms. Simpson 
states that from her review of the initial and revised plans, it appears as if the initial proposal was for 
an office use, but that the revised plans are clearly for server warehousing.  Mr. Krausche states that 
he has built many buildings, including retail spaces, and suggests that they are constantly in flux and
City of Salem Zoning Board of Appeals 
September 16, 2026 DRAFT Meeting Minutes 
  4 
changing depending on tenant use.  Mr. Krausche contends the actions taken here were standard 
practice regarding getting an initial permit.  He contends he has built more malls than anyone on this 
phone/zoom call and that nothing about the petitioner process was out of the ordinary or deceptive.   
 
Mr. Larrick notes that the application gave examples of banks and hospitals as other businesses that 
use similar technology, and he asks if in those cases the servers are in support of a larger business, 
whereas here the servers themselves seem to be the business.  Mr. Moser states the demand will 
dictate the number of servers and size, and states that this service will allow other companies to 
grow.  Mr. Ronan acknowledges that the service here is different than a bank or hospital, but that 
does not preclude it from being a business or service provider.  Mr. Larrick asks if there is any other 
use in the use table in the Zoning Ordinance that this would fit under if not for 
business/professional use, and Mr. Ronan states the petitioners feel strongly that this falls under that 
category.  Mr. Larrick asks additional clarifying questions, and notes there was a press release about 
Prime Group providing edge data centers as part of their business portfolio.  Mr. Moser explains the 
press release was about a change in business model to provide more for the local economy. 
 
Vice Chair McGaha asks further questions regarding primary versus accessory uses, noting the 
information provided in the initial petition for an IT services use.  She notes that the reduction to 
the staff room and increase in server spaces raises the question about changes in the principal use.  
Mr. Ronan clarifies that there was no reduction in staff area, just an additional buildout for servers 
and uninterruptible power supply.  Ms. McGaha clarifies that she meant a reduction in proportion to 
the overall square footage.  Mr. Ronan again argues that this qualifies as a business that sells a 
service, and that the Building Department does not have the power to arbitrarily say that they think 
a business is an AI data center versus an IT services company based on a criterion that is not 
expressed in the Zoning Ordinance.  He insists this was a mistake, and he asks that the Board 
correct that mistake with this appeal. 
 
The Board members and petitioners continue to discuss the matter of use, primary use, accessory 
use, and what is allowed.  The petitioners insist the use has not changed since the initial approval 
and permit.  Mr. Habib asks clarifying questions about the initial approval and described use, and 
Mr. Ronan indicates it was for an IT services company.  Mr. Larrick discusses the business category 
further and asks if there is a business that would not fall under the category of service.  There is a 
discussion of use categories and the fact that a data center does not currently exist.  There is also a 
discussion of what a data center is and various computing capacities, the need for cooling, and the 
scale at which the technologies use the resources of their space.  Mr. Ronan insists that this proposal 
is not what people fear in terms of resource use, energy use, noise, and other issues that other 
communities have faced with larger data centers.  Mr. Ronan contends there will be no additional 
power use beyond what is currently being used at the building and that municipal water will only be 
drawn upon for the bathroom and kitchen, not for cooling, as it will be a closed-loop system with 
delivery of off-site water.  With respect to heat and noise, Mr. Ronan states it will be minimal in an 
existing industrial building.  There is further discussion of business use and how the petition 
qualifies as a business or professional use, as well as scale.  Mr. Moser asks if cutting the server room 
in half would make the project more acceptable.  Chair Vyedin notes that one of the issues is that 
the ultimate end use of the space was not fully captured in the initial building permit, and that this 
ultimate use is not one in the table of allowed uses.  Mr. Moser states that he has many tenants in 
Shetland Park offering digital services and asks if he should tell them all to cease operating.  Ms. 
Vyedin suggests that servers providing inference are different than a company providing a digital 
service.  There is a continued discussion of the use and ultimate service provided by the petitioner,
City of Salem Zoning Board of Appeals

as well as the definition of “digital service”.  Mr. Moser continues to interrupt Chair Vyedin and 
suggests that she is making the petition sound like something it is not.  He insists this is a vital 
business service.   
 
Mr. Larrick next asks about generators on external pads in the initial plans.  Mr. Ronan states the 
initial plans had one generator, and now the revised plans have three generators to provide backup 
power, and two of the three go on existing pads.  Mr. Larrick questions whether the additional 
generator would be considered an accessory structure and require a special permit.  Mr. Moser states 
that if the generators are a concern, they are not necessary. 
   
The Board and petitioners continue to discuss the matter.  Chair Vyedin yields the floor to the Salem 
Building Department.   
 
Mr. Bennani introduces himself and clarifies that the City is not asking the Board to create a new use 
category, nor is it relying solely on the label “data center” in its decisions.  He states the question is 
based on the particular business and its functions and whether it fits the business or office 
professional category.  If the operation does not fit the category, then it is not as of right.  Mr. 
Bennani notes that after the expanded proposal, the Building Department determined the operation 
no longer fit the definition of business or professional office use.  He provides additional 
clarifications and explains that as more information came to light about what the initial proposal was 
with the expansion, it became apparent that this was not an allowed use.  Mr. Moser interrupts Mr. 
Bennani to suggest the City’s position is that any business offering a digital service is not an allowed 
use.  Chair Vyedin asks Mr. Moser to please refrain from interrupting, and Mr. Ronan confirms that 
the petitioner must not speak when he does not have the floor.  Mr. Bennani further explains why 
the permit was revoked rather than just the expansion being denied, stating again that it was because 
more information about the use came to light. 
 
Ms. Orfanos provides additional information regarding the Building Department’s authority as well 
as the facts that the Department became aware of with respect to the petition.  Ms. Kubik also 
provides details regarding the revocation of the permit and the timeline of events regarding the 
petitioner.  Ms. Kubik notes that the petitioner and their attorney have only been reading an 
incomplete definition of the use category and proceeds to read the full definition.  She discusses the 
definition of merchandise.  Ms. Kubik also indicates that the description of the business in the initial 
permit petition was an IT services office, but no further information was provided to support such 
claims.  She provides additional details and notes that if the petitioner has in fact begun demolition 
and construction pursuant to the pre-construction walk-through where the initial permit was 
revoked, then that would be a violation.  Ms. Kubik continues to discuss the question of use, as well 
as the total generator capacity being proposed and the zoning issues that arose from the additional 
proposed generators.  Chair Vyedin asks how much the petitioner paid for their permit, and Ms. 
Kubik states it was around $207,000.  The plan review process and permitting in general are 
discussed.  Ms. Kubik contends that the petitioner’s proposed use is a unique use that is not 
included in the use table.  The Board and Building Department staff continue to discuss the matter 
and timeline of events to date, with clarifications from the petitioner and staff. 
 
Chair Vyedin opens the floor to public comment. 
 
Kara McLaughlin introduces herself as the Chair of the Board at Salem Academy Charter School 
and states she does not have a stance as opposed or for the petition, but makes it clear that it is

important to make sure that children are safe, and she notes that there is a nearby public school with 
500 students.  Ms. McLaughlin asks the Board to review details in light of the proximity to students. 
 
Christina Fox introduces herself as a resident of Salem living on Loring Avenue and expresses 
opposition to the petition.  Ms. Fox asserts that the withdrawal and revocation of the permit should 
be upheld based on the various issues identified, and also notes there are several articles referencing 
the Prime Group’s expansion into AI data centers.  Ms. Fox also states that the definition of a data 
center is any facility that primarily contains electrical equipment used to process, store, and transmit 
digital information, which may be a free-standing structure or a facility within a larger structure, that 
uses environmental control equipment to maintain operation of that electrical equipment. 
 
Ward 6 City Councilor Katelyn Holappa introduces herself and states that the category “business or 
professional office use” cannot become a catch-all term for any use to be allowed by right in Salem 
as long as someone has a business case, because it would undermine zoning laws and create issues of 
ambiguity between commercial and industrial uses.  Ms. Holappa also expresses concerns about the 
power usage and heat output. 
 
Josh Manion of 7 Gables Circle introduces himself as the senior zoning review planner for the City 
of Somerville.  Mr. Manion expresses opposition to the petition and asks that the Board uphold the 
revocation of the building permit.  Mr. Manion suggests the proposal looks, feels, sounds, and acts 
like a data center.  
 
Lucy Corchado of 1 Chase Street introduces herself and expresses concerns about the petition 
relating to health and environmental impacts, particularly with respect to diesel generators and 
cooling infrastructure.  Ms. Corchado expresses dismay at the lack of transparency and suggests the 
revocation of the permit is warranted. 
 
Jim Lacy of 30 Sumner Road introduces himself and suggests that the words “as of right” should be 
stricken from the vocabulary of all humanity.  Mr. Lacy expresses concerns about the petition and 
what the ultimate end uses might be by the inference points. 
 
Tynah Hull introduces herself as a resident of Salem and a CEO of a software company.  Ms. Hull 
discusses IT services. 
 
Elisa Dhanger introduces herself as a resident of Salem on Tremont Street and expresses opposition 
to the petition.  Ms. Dhanger states it seems like pertinent information was not disclosed, and that 
the lack of transparency makes the revocation warranted.  She also speaks anecdotally about a 
business not being able to go through with plans due to disruption from a nearby data center.   
 
Kate (no last name or address provided) states her grandfather worked at a water generation plant 
with giant turbines providing electricity and that it was not an office.  She expresses concerns 
regarding noise from any potential data center and additional expansion, and suggests the appeal be 
denied. 
 
Sarah Wells of Ord Street introduces herself and states she supports denying the appeal.  Ms. Wells 
expresses concerns about potential wastewater associated with the cooling and the fact that the 
petition is to set up shop right next to the wharf.

Rebecca Love introduces herself and contests the petitioner’s claim that this is not a data center.  
She reads a definition of a data center and states that it is identical to what the petitioner is 
proposing.  Ms. Love states there should be no sidestepping of Zoning Ordinances and that this 
should be reviewed and permitted as a data center, not anything else. 
 
Timothy Paul introduces himself as a Salem resident off of Lafayette Street.  Mr. Paul states he is a 
lifelong resident of Salem and suggests it reflects poorly on Shetland Park that the petition lacked

Jennifer MacGregor introduces herself as a Salem resident and speaks in opposition to the petition.  
She suggests that if a party is hiding something, they are most likely doing something wrong, and

Adam Kaczmarek of Essex Street introduces himself and expresses concerns regarding the plans for 
additional buildout and use of additional and oversized generators.  Mr. Kaczmarek speaks against

A resident who provided no name or address states that AI and data centers have already proven to

Nathan Leshin of Carlton Street introduces himself and speaks against the proposal due to the

Phil Laffy of 1431 Fort Avenue introduces himself and states he is in favor of the proposal, 
suggesting that Attorney Ronan made valid points.  Mr. Laffy contends this is a service that is being

Lindsay Morsillo of 53 Broad Street introduces himself and suggests the issue here is scale.  Mr. 
Morsillo states it is a large amount of resources and density in a small space, and that he is opposed

Mack Normand introduces herself as a local community member and raises concerns about 
transparency and speaks against the proposal.

Carley Winn introduces herself and states that data centers create issues related to noise and suggests 
that having this on the water will merely exacerbate and echo the noise issue for residents and the 
fish. 
 
The petitioner is given an opportunity to respond to the comments.  Mr. Moser notes that the 
concerns about water are misplaced, as it is a closed-loop cooling system, and offers assurances that 
there would be noise mitigation measures and other lengths taken to ensure that the use is not a

The Board votes to close the public hearing.  Ms. McGaha motions to close the public hearing, and

The Board discusses the petition further and deliberates before bringing the matter to a vote.  The 
Board finds that the proposed use does not properly fall under the category of business or

Motion and Vote: Ms. Simpson motions to approve the petition of PRIME GROUP SHETLAND 
PARK, LLC and ALESSANDRO MAZZOTTA regarding the property located at 35 CONGRESS 
STREET, SHETLAND PARK BUILDING 2, UNIT 2120, (Map 34, Lot 0448) (Industrial Zoning 
District; Coastal Resiliency Overlay District; Waterfront Industrial Overlay District) to appeal the 
Building Commissioner’s decision to revoke a building permit for that property, including on the 
basis that the proposed use is a data center, a not permitted use per Section 3.1 Principal Uses of the 
Salem Zoning Ordinance. The petitioners contend that the proposed use is allowed as-of-right and 
the appeal requests that the Board: 1) reinstate the building permit to allow construction under the 
original scope of work, and 2) direct the Building Department to either review the expanded scope 
of work for building code compliance, or to review a new building permit application with 
instructions that the expanded scope of work cannot be denied based on the proposed use. 
 
Mr. Habib seconds the motion.  The vote is none (0) in favor and five (5) opposed (Christa 
McGaha, Ellen Simpson, Peter Habib, Stephen Larrick, and Nina Vyedin).  The motion 
does not pass.

Project: A public hearing for all persons interested in the petition of NICOLE ROBLERO at

Documents and Exhibitions     
 Application date-stamped ______, 2026 and supporting documentation 
 
Chair Vyedin introduces the petition. 
 
Brian Barrett introduces himself on behalf of the petitioner and discusses the proposal to keep the 
existing fence as constructed.  Mr. Barrett explains that the petitioner went to the Building 
Department years ago when originally seeking to build her fence, and was erroneously told that she 
did not need a permit.  Based on that, the petitioner built the fence in question.  After building the 
fence, the petitioner was informed she was in violation of City Zoning Ordinances for height and 
visibility.  The petitioner then sought a variance, but was denied, and Mr. Barrett indicates that was 
prior to the change in the variance standard.  Mr. Barrett argues that in this instance, the new 
standard of having a practical difficulty would apply, and seeks relief from the Board.  Mr. Barrett 
discusses the property and location, as well as the need for the fence, which is based on the 
petitioner having children and pets in the yard frequently and wanting to ensure safety.  Mr. Barrett
